{{Short description|Authenticated encryption mode of operation for block ciphers}}
'''Offset codebook mode''' ('''OCB mode''') is an [[authenticated encryption]] [[block cipher modes of operation|mode of operation]] for cryptographic [[block cipher]]s.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-krovetz-ocb/?include_text=1 | title=The OCB Authenticated-Encryption Algorithm | date=July 23, 2012 | access-date=May 28, 2012 | author=Ted Krovetz, Phillip Rogaway}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/ | title=OCB Mode | access-date=May 28, 2012 | author=Phillip Rogaway}}</ref>  OCB mode was designed by [[Phillip Rogaway]], who credits [[Mihir Bellare]], [[John Black (cryptographer)|John Black]], and Ted Krovetz with assistance and comments on the designs. It is based on the ''[[IAPM (mode)|integrity-aware parallelizeable mode]]'' (IAPM) of authenticated encryption by Charanjit S. Jutla.  The ''OCB2'' version was proven insecure, while the original ''OCB1'' as well as ''OCB3'' from 2011 are still considered secure.

==Encryption and authentication==
{{See also|Authenticated encryption}}

OCB mode was designed to provide both [[message authentication]] and [[privacy]]. It is essentially a scheme for integrating a [[message authentication code]] (MAC) into the operation of a [[block cipher]].  In this way, OCB mode avoids the need to use two systems: a MAC for authentication and [[encryption]] for confidentiality. This results in lower computational cost compared to using separate encryption and authentication functions.

There are three versions of OCB: OCB1, OCB2 and OCB3. OCB1 was published in 2001. OCB2 improves on OCB1 by allowing associated data to be included with the message, providing ''[[AEAD|authenticated encryption with associated data]]'' (AEAD; that is, data that are not encrypted but should be authenticated) and a new method for generating a sequence of offsets. OCB2 was first published in 2003, originally named ''authenticated-encryption mode'', or ''advanced encryption mode'' (''AEM'') and [[#Attacks|was shown to be completely insecure in 2019]]. OCB3, published in 2011, changes again the way offsets are computed and introduces minor performance improvements.

OCB2 was standardized in ISO/IEC{{nbsp}}19772:2009<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail?csnumber=46345 | title=ISO/IEC 19772:2009 Information technology -- Security techniques -- Authenticated encryption | publisher=ISO | date=2009-02-12 | access-date=May 28, 2012}}</ref> (although it was removed from the standard following the publication of the attack) and a modified OCB3 in RFC{{nbsp}}7253.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7253 |title=The OCB Authenticated-Encryption Algorithm |date=2014 |publisher=IETF |last1=Krovetz |first1=Ted |last2=Rogaway |first2=Phillip }}</ref> The RFC encodes the tag length into the internally formatted nonce.

==Performance==
OCB performance overhead is minimal compared to classical, non-authenticating modes like [[cipher block chaining]]. OCB requires one block cipher operation per block of encrypted and authenticated message, and one block cipher operation per block of associated data. There is also one extra block cipher operation required at the end of process.

For comparison, [[CCM mode]] offering similar functionality requires twice as many block cipher operations per message block (associated data requires one, as in OCB).

==Patents==

While OCB is now public domain, Rogaway initially patented OCB mode so that he could charge for commercial licenses and in attempt to stop his work showing up in military-related projects.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rogaway |first1=Philip |title=OCB - An Authenticated-Encryption Scheme - Licensing - Rogaway |url=https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/license.htm |website=www.cs.ucdavis.edu |access-date=31 July 2023}}</ref> Rogaway intentionally abandoned his OCB patents in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=OCB patents are abandoned; freely usable|url=https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/cfrg/qLTveWOdTJcLn4HP3ev-vrj05Vg/|access-date=2021-02-27|website=mailarchive.ietf.org| author=Phillip Rogaway}}</ref>

Two U.S. patents were issued for OCB mode.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/ocb-faq.htm#patent:phil | title=OCB FAQ - Is OCB Patented | access-date=May 28, 2012 | author=Phillip Rogaway}}</ref> The patents have hindered approval by the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]].{{citation_needed|date=July 2023}}

While OCB mode was patented, Rogaway made three licenses available to allow OCB mode to be freely used in software licensed under the [[GNU General Public License]] (later any open source license certified by the [[Open Source Initiative]]<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/license.htm | title=OCB: free licenses | date=9 January 2013 | author=Phillip Rogaway}}</ref>), non-commercial non-military projects, and in [[OpenSSL]]. 

Since Rogaway only applied for patent protection in the U.S., the algorithm has always been free to use in software not developed and not sold inside the U.S.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/offer.htm | title=OCB: Offer Letter | date=29 March 2005 | access-date=May 28, 2012 | author=Phillip Rogaway}}</ref>

==Attacks==
[[Niels Ferguson]] pointed out [[Collision attack|collision attacks]] on OCB, which limits the amount of data that can be securely processed under a single key to about 280 terabytes.<ref>
{{cite web
 | url=http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/toolkit/BCM/documents/comments/General_Comments/papers/Ferguson.pdf
 | title=Collision attacks on OCB
 | author=Niels Ferguson
 | date=2002-02-11
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/ocb/ocb-faq.htm#ferguson
 | title= OCB: Background
 | author=Phillip Rogaway
 | date=2015-02-27
}}</ref>

In October 2018, Inoue and Minematsu presented an [[existential forgery attack]] against OCB2 that requires only a single prior encryption query and almost no computational power or storage.<ref>
{{cite web
 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1040
 | title=Cryptanalysis of OCB2
 | author=Akiko Inoue and Kazuhiko Minematsu
 | date=2018-10-26
}}</ref> The attack does not extend to OCB1 or OCB3, and it requires that the associated data field of the forged ciphertext be empty. Poettering<ref>
{{cite web
 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1087
 | title=Breaking the confidentiality of OCB2
 | author=Bertram Poettering
 | date=2018-11-08
}}</ref> and Iwata<ref>
{{cite web
 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1090
 | title=Plaintext Recovery Attack of OCB2
 | author=Tetsu Iwata
 | date=2018-11-11
}}</ref> improved the forgery attack to a full plaintext recovery attack just a couple of days later. The four authors later produced a joint report.<ref name="OCB2-2019">
{{cite web
 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/311
 | title=Cryptanalysis of OCB2: Attacks on Authenticity and Confidentiality
 | date=2019-03-19
 | first1 = Akiko | last1= Inoue | first2= Tetsu |last2= Iwata |first3= Kazuhiko | last3= Minematsu | first4= Bertram | last4= Poettering
}}</ref>
